content: Iron John is a German fairy tale included in the Brothers Grimm collection, specifically tale number 136. It narrates the story of a wild man and a prince. The original German title, Eisenhans, combines Eisen, meaning iron, and Hans, a common short form of the name Johannes, akin to John in English. This tale is classified as Aarne-Thompson type 502, The Wild Man as a Helper. Many interpret the story as an allegory for a boy's journey into adulthood. The tale also inspired the book Iron John: A Book About Men, which played a significant role in the Men's Movement of the early 1990s. The story begins with a king who sends a huntsman into a nearby forest, but the huntsman never returns. The king sends more huntsmen, but they too disappear. Eventually, the king dispatches all his remaining huntsmen as a group, but none return. Declaring the forest dangerous, the king forbids anyone from entering it. Years later, a wandering explorer and his dog hear of the forest's dangers and request permission to hunt there, claiming he might uncover the fate of the missing hunters. While exploring, the dog is nearly dragged underwater by a massive arm in a lake at the forest's center. The explorer returns the next day with a group of men to drain the lake. They discover a naked man with iron-like skin and long, shaggy hair covering his body. The wild man is captured and locked in a cage in the king's courtyard as a curiosity. The king decrees that anyone who frees the wild man will face death. Years later, the young prince is playing with a ball in the courtyard. The ball accidentally rolls into the wild man's cage. The wild man picks it up and refuses to return it unless he is set free. He reveals that the only key to the cage is hidden beneath the queen's pillow. Initially hesitant, the prince eventually musters the courage to sneak into his mother's room and steal the key. He releases the wild man, who introduces himself as Iron John (or Iron Hans, depending on the translation). Fearing punishment for freeing Iron John, the prince agrees to accompany him into the forest. Iron John, a powerful being guarding many treasures, tasks the prince with watching over a well. He warns the prince not to let anything touch or fall into the well, as it will instantly turn to gold. The prince obeys at first but eventually plays in the well, turning all his hair to gold. Disappointed by the boy's failure, Iron John sends him away to experience poverty and hardship. However, he tells the prince that if he ever needs help, he should call Iron John's name three times. The prince travels to a distant kingdom and offers his services to its king. Ashamed of his golden hair, he keeps his cap on in the king's presence and is assigned to assist the gardener. When war threatens the kingdom, the prince seizes the opportunity to prove himself. He calls upon Iron John, who provides him with a horse, armor, and a legion of iron warriors. The prince successfully defends the kingdom but returns everything he borrowed to Iron John before resuming his humble position. In celebration, the king announces a banquet and offers his daughter's hand in marriage to any knight who can catch a golden apple thrown into their midst. Hoping to identify the mysterious knight who saved the kingdom, the king uses this challenge as a lure. The prince again seeks Iron John's help, who disguises him as the mysterious knight. The prince catches the golden apple and escapes, repeating this feat on two more occasions. Eventually, his identity is discovered. The prince is restored to his former status, marries the princess, and is joyfully reunited with his parents. Iron John also attends the wedding, now free of the hair and iron skin that once made him fearsome. He reveals that he had been under an enchantment, which could only be broken by someone worthy and pure of heart who would set him free. This tale has numerous variants across Europe, such as The Hairy Man. A broader variant, found in Europe, Asia, and Africa, begins with the prince serving an evil being, from whom he gains similar gifts, and the story proceeds similarly. One such tale is The Magician's Horse. The oldest preserved variant is the Italian Guerrino and the Savage Man. Another notable version is Georgic and Merlin.
